description.narrative:
The Power of Voices Partnership (PvP) is an influencing programme with the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The programme FAIR for ALL led by Oxfam Novib is five year long initiative implemented jointly with consortium members Huairou Commission, SOMO and Third World Network-Africa (TWN-Africa) aimed at supporting and collaborating with people’s rightful demands towards companies, governments and multilateral organizations for economic, social and environmental justice, promoting global trade and value-chains that are fair for all. The main focus of the FAIR for ALL programme proposal is to support and strengthen CSOs to play their diverse roles; as educators, mobilizers, creators and watchdogs to make trade and value chains FAIR for ALL.
In South Africa FAIR for ALL programme aims at a strengthened civil society capable of creating space and mobilizing people to achieve structural and gender transformative changes to South Africa’s economic model and legislative frameworks to end gendered inequalities and contribute to more sustainable and inclusive mining and agricultural value chains that deliver wealth and benefits for all. The South Africa FAIR for ALL programme will to implemented by SOMO, Oxfam South Africa and partners, and Third World Network-Africa and partners.
The South Africa FAIR for ALL programme will be implemented by Oxfam South Africa, Third World Network-Africa and partners. Oxfam South Africa willfocus on the following, 1) Support local civil society, especially women and their communities, to collect evidence on rights abuses (and more specifically research linkages between bulk production and rights abuses) and to get redress or compensation such as access to free or affordable health care, an end to evictions, and women’s ownership of dignified housing on farms. 2) Support civil society to engage with government to ensure a responsible private and financial sector that values the common good and upholds women’srights – including rights related to owning SMEs, dignified work and living wages – and environmental rights. 3) Support women-owned SMEs, particularly small-scale agricultural producers and artisanal miners, to come together in cooperatives, networks and movements to co-create alternative business models (for SMEs) that contribute to women’s economic empowerment and 135 Universal Periodic Review of South Africa. 4) Supporting local civil society and network building to advocate for the government to reform the mining sector, promoting alternative more sustainable economic models and new types of job.
These objectives will be achieved by strengthening local civil society in South Africa through, • Building organizational development to strengthen women and their collective power.• A better understanding of obstacles and opportunities for women in agricultural value chains. • Sensitizing women in value chainsabout their rights and increasing their negotiating and advocacy skills to effectively claim those rights.
To achieve main objectives of the programme, Oxfam will collaborate with the following organisations, •Centre for Competition, Regulation and Economic Development (CCRED): has nine years’ experience building knowledge through rigorous evidence-based research on key issues of competition, regulation, industrial development and the conduct of large firms, specifically related to regional development in Southern and East Africa. • The Graça Machel Trust: engages directly with women to empower them. Amplifies women’s movements by harnessing and promoting their contributions to the economic, social, and political development of Africa. • Tshintsha Amakhaya (TA): means ‘improving livelihoods’ in isiZulu and isiXhosa; a civil society alliance of ten NGOs with longstanding experience in land and agrarian reform,labour rights of farm workers, and supporting rural social movements. They have supported rural people’s struggles through joint campaigns on access to land, gender equality and climate justice.

participating-org.narrative: Oxfam South Africa is an independent Oxfam affiliate who manages and implements the programme of Oxfam in South Africa. Its programme prioritises vulnerable communities and creating lasting change in, and for all the people in South Africa. Oxfam South Africa works in partnership with organisations who seek to create meaningful and sustainable change that benefits vulnerable groups in South Africa through the attainment, protection and preservation of human rights and social justice. The country program will continue to focus its work through ‘active citizenship and accountability’ and ‘gender justice’ lenses.

"Two GAP (Good Agricultural Practices) workshops were held in Eastern Cape one in East London (17 women) and another in Mthatha (24 women, some virtual). The purpose was to equip women farmers with the knowledge and tools to meet food safety, traceability, and hygiene standards, which are prerequisites for accessing local and export markets. The workshops included modules on worker welfare, environmental protection, and record-keeping. These trainings directly supported participants’ readiness to enter formal markets.WFP facilitated a series of two-day workshops for women working on various farms. These workshops covered key labour-related topics such as Sectoral Determination, Dismissals, the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act (COIDA), Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF), and Case Work Management, among others.To enrich the learning experience, WFP invited officials from the Department of Employment and Labour (DEL) and the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration (CCMA) to participate. This created a valuable platform for women to engage directly with officials, raise concerns, and highlight rights violations they face in their workplaces.The workshops were grounded in a participatory, interactive methodology inspired by the Training for Transformation (TfT) approach. This ensured that women's lived experiences remained central to the process, and their active participation was encouraged throughout the sessions.The Just Agriculture Transition and Food Sovereignty Movement was formed out of a national Indaba held in Mthatha, Eastern Cape, in November 2024, organized by the South Africa consortium partners as part of the Fair4All project. The Indaba brought together small-scale farmers, farm workers, backyard gardeners,grassroots leaders, and civil society organizations to address injustices in agricultural value chains and envision a more just and sustainable agricultural future. Rooted in the slogan “Food Sovereignty in Our Life

description.narrative: CSOs demonstrating increased expertise on Value chains specific to project

comment.narrative: CCRED produced three value chain assessment reports following their research that serve as practical strategies to address production and market access constraints as key to unlocking greater opportunities for women-run businesses. At the core of the reports is a deepened gender lens perspective that isolates and systematically assess gender-specific constraints on entry and participation of women-run businesses. The different research outputs highlighted key areas for intervention including where and how existing policy tools could be used to further improve participation of SMEs and women-owned businesses.

Through the research conducted by CCRED in Year 1, they developed and provided a training for multi-stakeholders (CSOs, SMMEs in the agriculture and agro-business sectors, academics, etc) on Competition law and Policy and shared the findings from the research they conducted on Barriers to entry of women to markets on the poultry, vegetable and fruits value chains. Outcome: increased knowledge on how to navigate the complexities related to entry of women to the poultry, vegetable and fruits value chains and institutions to consult when faced with challenges.
Through the research conducted on the agriculture and agro-processing sectors (AAMP) for the Agriculture Agro-processing Master Plan in year 1, CCRED has demonstrated increased expertise on value chains. OZA invited CCRED to train the AAMP Working Group on the developments of the social compact, highlight the opportunities available to access and influence this space. Outcome: the members of the AAMP Working Group were more informed about the Social Compact and have a better clarity on how the AAMP can be used to measure the progress of the commitments made by government departments in promoting economic growth and access by different stakeholders such as small-scale farmers, SMEs, Afro-preneurs tofinancing, markets, key networks, etc.

"Collaborations have been established with Eastern Cape Development Corporation (ECDC), African Farmers Association of South Africa (AFASA), Women in Rural and Agriculture Development (WARD), National African Federated Chamber of Commerce (NAFCOC), Nelson Mandela Bay Chamber of Business. The African Women in Agribusiness Network (AWAB) is supported by a strategically diverse group of organizations—National African Federated Chamber of Commerce and Industry (NAFCOC), Women in Agriculture and Rural Development (WARD), African Farmers’ Association of South Africa – Women’s Chapter (AFASA Women), Nelson Mandela Bay Business Chamber, and the Eastern Cape Development Corporation (ECDC)—each contributing unique and complementary expertise. Together, they offer AWAB a powerful mix of grassroots reach, policy influence, enterprise development, and market access. AFASA Women and WARD provide deep knowledge of smallholder farming and women’s leadership, while NAFCOC strengthens advocacy for inclusive economic participation and land governance. The Nelson Mandela Bay Business Chamber brings private sector insight and SME competitiveness, and ECDC offers access to government-backed enterprise support and funding opportunities. This collective ensures that AWAB is notonly a platform for knowledge exchange, but also a vehicle for structural transformation in agricultural value chains by amplifying the voice, visibility, and viability of black women agripreneurs"

Standard Bank provides support to One Farm Share to enable them to facilitate small-scale farmers access to markets through the Hello choice Digital Platform and ensuring that their produce is purchased and collected on a weekly basis. Results: a) This model advances food security, sustainability of small-scale farmers (market-related prices were secured, transport was provided to collect the produce from farmers, packaging support was provided) and opened up opportunities for small-scale farmers to innovate. b) Before this initiative was put in place small-scale farmers struggled with access to market given rural location and were often constrained by physical limitation of carrying produce to roadside stalls. c) A notable improvement in farming activities including land prep and crop management. d) 29 farmers received agronomy and business support

Oxfam South Africa together with 13 community representatives from the mining and agricultural sectors participated in the Alternative Mining Indaba that was hosted in Cape Town on the 9-11 May 2022. This forum provided space for CSOs including mining communities to engage with for example Anglo America on their plans to advance the implementation of Just Energy Transitions in Africa. Mining communities shared their concerns regarding the lack of implementation of Free, Prior, Informed Consent (FPIC) and highlighted how they would like to be engaged by Anglo American Gold. Anglo American Gold noted the recommendations from the mining communities and other participants (such as academics, CSOs, etc) and set timelines for them to respond to them. 300 in-person and 200 virtual. "WFP mobilised 25 new members: In September 2022, WFP undertook recruitment visits and meetings to various “new” farms in Stellenbosch, Simondium, and Paarl. Recruitment entailed identifying “new” farms (i.e. farms on which WFP has never worked and on which other organisations and trade unions are not working); making initial contact with a few women on the farm; making arrangements to return to the farm to meet with a bigger group of women farm workers; introducing WFP and explaining the F4A programme; understanding the working and living conditions on that farm; determining women’s interest to become active on the F4A programme. Such recruitment meetings typically took place over a number of repeat visits to the same farm, usually in the evenings or over weekends, in order to build trust and relationships with the women.
